t: What a Magnetic Parts Tray Is and Why Builders Use One
title: What a Magnetic Parts Tray Is and Why Builders Use One
description: A magnetic parts tray is a shallow steel dish or plate with a magnet in its base that holds screws, standoffs, washers, and other small ferrous hardware in place on the workbench. During a PC build it keeps tiny motherboard screws and M.2 standoffs from rolling off the desk and getting lost. The tray sits within arm's reach while you work, and every screw you remove goes straight into it, so nothing vanishes under the case.

t: How the Base Magnet Holds Hardware in Place
title: How the Base Magnet Holds Hardware in Place
description: Most trays use a ferrite or rubber magnet bonded under a stainless-steel dish. The magnetic field passes through the thin steel and pins each screw flat against the dish surface, so screws stay put even if the tray is bumped. Typical holding strength keeps 30 to 60 screws from sliding, though the pull is gentle enough that you can still pick screws up with your fingers. Rubber-coated bases add a non-slip grip on the desk.

demo.program:
import math
screw_weight_g = 0.5          # typical M3 screw
tray_pull_g = 2500            # typical rubber-magnet tray pull
n_screws = 50
load_g = screw_weight_g * n_screws
print("Tray rated pull: %dg | load of %d screws: %dg" % (tray_pull_g, n_screws, load_g))
print("Safety factor: %.1fx" % (tray_pull_g / load_g))
print("Bump-proof: yes" if tray_pull_g / load_g > 10 else "Bump-proof: marginal")

t: Standard Sizes: 4-Inch Round, 6-Inch Round, and Rectangular Trays
title: Standard Sizes: 4-Inch Round, 6-Inch Round, and Rectangular Trays
description: The classic magnetic parts tray is a round dish about 4 inches (10 cm) across and 1 inch deep — big enough for a full motherboard's worth of screws. Six-inch (15 cm) rounds hold entire teardown screw sets, while rectangular trays (roughly 5.5 by 3.5 inches) fit more hardware in a smaller desk footprint and slide neatly beside the case. Deeper 1.5-inch walls suit chunky standoffs and GPU bracket screws.

demo.program:
trays = [("4-inch round", 4.0, 25), ("6-inch round", 6.0, 60), ("rect 5.5x3.5", 5.5, 45)]
screw_set = 40
for name, size, cap in trays:
    print(f"{name:>14}: capacity ~{cap} screws -> {'FITS 40-screw set' if cap >= screw_set else 'too small'}")

t: Round vs Square vs Rectangular Tray Shapes
title: Round vs Square vs Rectangular Tray Shapes
description: Round trays are the most common and cheapest, and their curved rim funnels screws to the center. Square trays tile neatly into bench organizers and drawer dividers. Rectangular trays give the best screws-per-square-inch and leave a corner free for a magnetized screwdriver. For PC building, a rectangular tray next to the case plus a small round one inside the case footprint is a popular two-tray setup.

t: Materials: Stainless Steel Dishes vs Plastic Magnetic Pads
title: Materials: Stainless Steel Dishes vs Plastic Magnetic Pads
description: Stainless-steel trays are the standard: the magnet acts through the steel, the surface wipes clean, and they last for years. Plastic trays with a magnetic pad insert are lighter and will not scratch glass desks, but their hold is weaker and the pad can peel with age. Silicone screw mats are the non-magnetic alternative — great for organizing by zone, but they will not save a screw that rolls off the edge.

demo.program:
mats = [("stainless steel", 9, "strong, durable, wipeable"),
        ("plastic + magnetic pad", 5, "light, weaker hold"),
        ("silicone screw mat", 0, "non-magnetic, zone organizing")]
print("Material comparison (hold score 0-10):")
for m, score, note in mats:
    print(f"  {m:<24} hold={score}/10  {note}")

t: Holding Strength Classes and What They Mean in Practice
title: Holding Strength Classes and What They Mean in Practice
description: Entry trays (around 5 dollars) use a basic rubber magnet that holds a motherboard's screw set on a flat desk. Mid-range trays add a stronger ceramic magnet that keeps screws pinned when the tray is tilted. Heavy-duty trays with neodymium magnets can hold screws upside down, but they magnetize nearby screwdrivers — handy or annoying depending on the job. Match strength to need: flat-bench work needs only the basic class.

demo.program:
classes = [("basic rubber", 1.0, "flat desk work"),
           ("ceramic", 2.5, "tilted trays, lap work"),
           ("neodymium", 8.0, "vertical/inverted hold")]
base = 2500
for name, mult, use in classes:
    print(f"{name:<14} pull ~{int(base*mult)}g  best for: {use}")

t: Magnetic Safety Around PC Parts: SSDs, HDDs, and USB Drives
title: Magnetic Safety Around PC Parts: SSDs, HDDs, and USB Drives
description: The weak field of a parts tray is harmless to SSDs, USB flash drives, RAM, and CPUs — flash memory is not magnetic storage. Keep the tray a few inches from spinning mechanical hard drives as a precaution, since strong fields can disturb their servo tracks. Never store the tray pressed against credit-card stripes or mechanical watch movements. For a normal PC build, tray-on-desk is completely safe for every component you handle.

demo.program:
safe = ["SSD", "NVMe drive", "USB flash", "RAM", "CPU", "GPU"]
caution = ["spinning HDD (keep 3+ inches away)", "magnetic stripe cards"]
print("Safe next to tray:", ", ".join(safe))
print("Keep distance from:", "; ".join(caution))

t: Use Case: Motherboard Standoff and Mounting Screw Workflow
title: Use Case: Motherboard Standoff and Mounting Screw Workflow
description: Mounting a motherboard means nine standoffs plus nine matching screws, and dropping one inside the case wastes ten minutes. The workflow: count nine standoffs into the tray, install them, then count nine screws into the tray and drive them in order. Any screw left in the tray after the board is seated is a flag — one position was missed. The tray turns screw counting into a built-in error check.

demo.program:
standoffs_needed, screws_needed = 9, 9
tray = {"standoffs": 9, "screws": 9}
installed_s, installed_c = 9, 8
leftover = tray["screws"] - installed_c
print(f"Standoffs: {installed_s}/{standoffs_needed} OK")
print(f"Screws: {installed_c}/{screws_needed} -> {leftover} left in tray = MISSED POSITION")

t: Use Case: M.2 SSD Screws and Other Tiny Fasteners
title: Use Case: M.2 SSD Screws and Other Tiny Fasteners
description: M.2 screws are the easiest fasteners to lose in a PC build — a single 2 mm screw can vanish into carpet forever. Drop it in the magnetic tray the moment the motherboard box opens, before touching the drive. The magnet holds it flat and visible against the steel, and the tray's rim stops it rolling. Builders who tray every tiny screw report essentially zero lost-fastener incidents.

demo.program:
tiny = ["M.2 screw", "M.2 standoff", "WiFi card screw", "CMOS jumper cap"]
print("Tray rule: tiny hardware goes in the tray FIRST, before it is handled.")
for i, part in enumerate(tiny, 1):
    print(f"  zone {i}: {part} (magnet holds flat, rim blocks rolling)")

t: Buying Guide: What to Check Before You Buy a Parts Tray
title: Buying Guide: What to Check Before You Buy a Parts Tray
description: Check five things: a rubber or PVC-coated base so it does not slide or scratch; a magnet strong enough that screws do not migrate when you bump the bench; a rim at least 3/4 inch tall; a size that fits your bench (4-inch round for tight desks); and stainless steel you can wipe thermal paste off. Expect 5 to 15 dollars. Two trays — one for screws in, one for screws out — beats one big tray for teardowns.

demo.program:
criteria = [("non-slip rubber base", True), ("rim >= 0.75 in", True),
            ("stainless dish", True), ("price <= $15", True), ("second tray for teardowns", False)]
score = sum(1 for _, ok in criteria if ok)
for name, ok in criteria:
    print(("PASS " if ok else "FAIL ") + name)
print(f"Buy score: {score}/{len(criteria)}")

t: Cleaning and Maintenance: Metal Filings and Paste Smears
title: Cleaning and Maintenance: Metal Filings and Paste Smears
description: Steel trays collect fine metal filings from case edges and screw threads — wipe them out with a dry cloth before each build, because filings can bridge motherboard contacts. Thermal paste smears come off stainless with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth. If the rubber base gets dusty and slides, wash it with soap and water and let it dry. A tray needs no lubrication and has no parts to wear out.

demo.program:
tasks = [("wipe metal filings (dry cloth)", "before every build"),
         ("clean paste smears (IPA + lint-free)", "as needed"),
         ("wash rubber base (soap + water)", "when it slides")]
print("Maintenance schedule:")
for t, when in tasks:
    print(f"  - {t}: {when}")
print("Wear parts: none. Expected life: years.")

t: Magnetic Tray vs Silicone Screw Mat vs Pill Organizer
title: Magnetic Tray vs Silicone Screw Mat vs Pill Organizer
description: Magnetic trays win on bump-resistance and one-hand screw pickup. Silicone screw mats win on zone labeling — you can write position numbers beside each screw pile, which trays cannot do. Pill organizers win on sealed transport but are slow to load. The practical answer for PC work: a magnetic tray for active screws plus a silicone mat with drawn zones for teardown mapping. Each covers the other's weakness.

title: Two-Tray and Multi-Tray Workstation Layouts
description: Serious builders run a tray system: tray one holds screws coming out of the old configuration, tray two stages screws for the new one, and a third small tray parks the current step's hardware within reach of the case. Color-coding helps — a red tray for removed screws, a blue tray for new screws. During a full rebuild this layout cuts screw-handling time roughly in half versus a single pile.

demo.program:
layout = [("red tray (left)", "screws REMOVED from old config"),
          ("blue tray (right)", "screws STAGED for new config"),
          ("small tray (at case)", "CURRENT step hardware")]
print("Three-tray bench layout:")
for tray, role in layout:
    print(f"  {tray:<22} -> {role}")

t: Pro Technique: Magnetizing Screwdriver Tips With the Tray
title: Pro Technique: Magnetizing Screwdriver Tips With the Tray
description: A strong tray magnet doubles as a screwdriver magnetizer: stroke the bit across the tray's magnet a few times in one direction and the bit becomes weakly magnetic, holding screws on the tip for blind installs. The charge fades over days, and a few reverse strokes (or a demagnetizer) remove it. Do not magnetize bits you use near magnetic-stripe cards or compass-sensitive work — keep one dedicated magnetized driver instead.

demo.program:
strokes = 6
charge = min(100, strokes * 15)
print(f"After {strokes} one-direction strokes across the tray magnet:")
print(f"  tip charge ~{charge}% (holds M3 screw on tip)")
print("  fades over ~3-5 days; reverse strokes remove it")

title: Complete Build-Station Screw Management System
description: The master workflow combines everything: one rectangular tray staged with the new build's full screw set counted in advance, one round tray catching every screw removed during disassembly, a silicone zone mat mapping teardown positions, and a photographed tray layout as the reassembly reference. Count in, count out, photograph, and no build ever ends with mystery screws — the tray system is the whole quality gate for fastener handling.

demo.program:
plan = [("stage", "count full new-build screw set into rect tray"),
        ("catch", "every removed screw -> round tray, never the desk"),
        ("map", "teardown positions on silicone zone mat"),
        ("verify", "photograph trays; count in == count out")]
print("Master screw workflow:")
for step, action in plan:
    print(f"  [{step:^6}] {action}")
print("Result: zero mystery screws, zero lost fasteners.")
